course_information.title: Inventory Management Fundamentals
course_information.description: Learn how products move through a hardware store, how inventory records support customer service, and how to handle common stock questions accurately.
course_information.intended_audience: All employees; especially receiving, stocking, sales floor, and inventory associates
course_information.scope: General; store-specific policies must be supplied separately
course_information.restrictions: No authority to perform inventory adjustments, investigations, detentions, security review, equipment operation, or price overrides without store authorization.
learning_objectives: Explain on-hand, available, and on-order inventory in plain language.
Describe the basic receiving-to-sale inventory flow.
Identify safe and accurate steps when receiving or stocking products.
Respond appropriately when shelf stock and inventory records disagree.
Recognize when to escalate adjustments, damaged items, or discrepancies.

lessons.title: Inventory Is More Than What Is on the Shelf
lessons.objective: Understand what inventory records mean and why accuracy matters.
lessons.why_this_matters: Inventory is the merchandise a store has for sale. A product may be in the aisle, in a back room, on a display, or waiting to be received. The computer record is useful, but it is not a promise that an item is ready for a customer to take home.

content_sections.heading: Three useful numbers
content_sections.text: On-hand means the quantity recorded as physically owned or held by the store. Available means the quantity that can be sold now under the store’s system rules. On-order means units expected from a supplier. These numbers can differ because of holds, pending transactions, receiving delays, or errors.

content_sections.heading: Why it matters
content_sections.text: An incorrect count can lead to a missed sale, an unnecessary reorder, or a disappointed customer. Verify the item, size, and location before promising it is available.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks for twelve 3-inch deck screws in a specific package. The system shows twelve packages on hand, but only eight are on the shelf. The associate checks approved alternate locations and asks for help before promising twelve.
what_to_say_or_do: Confirm the exact SKU, size, and package quantity.
Check the approved inventory view and the shelf location.
Explain what you can verify, not what you assume.
common_mistakes: Treating an on-hand count as a guarantee of availability.
Promising incoming stock before it is received.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask the inventory lead when a count, reservation, or shipment status is unclear.

supporting_materials.purpose: Only use a verified product or shelf photograph if it improves understanding.
supporting_materials.accessibility: Provide alt text identifying the relevant product/location and instructional point.

key_takeaways: Confirm the exact SKU, size, and package quantity.
Check the approved inventory view and the shelf location.
Ask the inventory lead when a count, reservation, or shipment status is unclear.

practice.question: A system shows 10 on hand, but only 6 are visible. What should you tell a customer?

options.text: Ten are definitely ready to buy.
You can verify six now and check for the others.
Tell the customer to return tomorrow.

practice.explanation: The visible six can be verified. Check other approved locations before promising more.

lessons.title: Follow a Product from Delivery to Sale
lessons.objective: Describe the main steps in the inventory flow.
lessons.why_this_matters: A product usually enters through an order and delivery. It is checked, received in the approved system, labeled or located, stocked, sold, and replenished when needed. Each step depends on accurate information from the previous step.

content_sections.heading: Receiving is a checkpoint
content_sections.text: Compare delivered products with the store’s receiving paperwork or system. Confirm product identity, units, and quantities. Record exceptions using the store’s process. Do not assume every box contains the expected item.

content_sections.heading: Stocking supports finding
content_sections.text: Place items in the correct approved location with readable labels. Keep the product identifier connected to the right shelf tag. A product placed in the wrong bay can appear missing even when it is in the building.

content_sections.heading: Sales update records
content_sections.text: A completed sale usually changes the system’s stock record. Returns, transfers, damage, and corrections may also change counts. Exact timing and permissions depend on the store’s software.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A carton marked “12” contains twelve individual hinges, but the store sells them in packs of two. The receiver checks the SKU and unit of measure before entering a quantity.
what_to_say_or_do: Check the item identifier and unit of measure.
Set aside and report mismatches instead of guessing.
common_mistakes: Receiving by carton count when the system expects eaches.
Putting merchandise out before resolving an item mismatch.
Leaving an unreadable shelf label in place.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a trained receiver or manager before posting a questionable receipt or correction.

supporting_materials.purpose: Only use a verified product or shelf photograph if it improves understanding.
supporting_materials.accessibility: Provide alt text identifying the relevant product/location and instructional point.

key_takeaways: Check the item identifier and unit of measure.
Ask a trained receiver or manager before posting a questionable receipt or correction.

practice.question: A carton holds 12 individual pieces, but the system expects packs of two. What comes first?

options.text: Verify the SKU and unit of measure.

practice.explanation: The unit of measure determines how the quantity should be entered.

lessons.title: Stock Shelves with Accuracy and Care
lessons.objective: Apply basic stocking practices that protect people and inventory accuracy.
lessons.why_this_matters: Good stocking makes products easier to find and reduces avoidable mistakes. It also keeps aisles usable and prevents damage. Follow the store’s safety rules and do not use equipment you are not authorized to operate.

content_sections.heading: Match the label
content_sections.text: Read the SKU, size, color, and package count. Similar-looking products can be different. Compare the product to the shelf tag before placing it.

content_sections.heading: Keep stock organized
content_sections.text: Use the store’s rotation rules when they apply. Keep heavy products in approved locations. Do not block exits, fire equipment, or customer walkways.

content_sections.heading: Watch for damage
content_sections.text: Do not place leaking, broken, or unsafe products on the sales floor. Follow the store’s process for isolating and reporting them.

lessons.hardware_store_example: Two boxes of similar faucet connectors have different lengths. An associate checks both labels rather than placing them together behind one shelf tag.
what_to_say_or_do: Match product and shelf tag before stocking.
Keep merchandise within approved shelf limits.
common_mistakes: Hiding extra product in an unrecorded location.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask for help with high, heavy, leaking, damaged, or uncertain merchandise.

supporting_materials.purpose: Only use a verified product or shelf photograph if it improves understanding.
supporting_materials.accessibility: Provide alt text identifying the relevant product/location and instructional point.

key_takeaways: Match product and shelf tag before stocking.
Keep merchandise within approved shelf limits.
Ask for help with high, heavy, leaking, damaged, or uncertain merchandise.

practice.question: Two packages look alike but have different lengths. What is the best next step?

options.text: Put both behind the same tag.
Check each product identifier against its location.

practice.explanation: The item identifier prevents a wrong-location error.

lessons.title: Investigate Inventory Differences
lessons.objective: Use a repeatable approach when shelf counts and system records differ.
lessons.why_this_matters: A discrepancy is a difference between what the system says and what staff can verify. A missing item does not always mean theft. It may be in another location, not yet received, sold under another identifier, or counted in the wrong unit.

content_sections.heading: Start with the exact item
content_sections.text: Check the SKU and unit of measure. Look at approved shelf, display, back-stock, and hold locations. Review available transaction details only if your role permits.

content_sections.heading: Record what you found
content_sections.text: Use the store’s approved count or discrepancy process. State the quantity you physically verified and where you checked. Do not quietly change records or accuse anyone.

content_sections.heading: Escalate adjustments
content_sections.text: Inventory adjustments can affect ordering and financial records. Only authorized employees should make them.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A paint roller refill shows six on hand but none in its assigned bay. The associate checks the endcap and back-stock location, then reports the discrepancy with the SKU.
what_to_say_or_do: Document findings and request an authorized adjustment if needed.
common_mistakes: Counting a similar item as the missing SKU.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask the inventory manager before any count correction, suspected loss investigation, or unexplained variance.

supporting_materials.purpose: Only use a verified product or shelf photograph if it improves understanding.
supporting_materials.accessibility: Provide alt text identifying the relevant product/location and instructional point.

key_takeaways: Ask the inventory manager before any count correction, suspected loss investigation, or unexplained variance.

practice.question: You find a count mismatch. What should you do first?

options.text: Verify the SKU and approved locations.

practice.explanation: Check identity and locations before escalating a documented discrepancy.

lessons.title: Help Customers with Stock Questions
lessons.objective: Communicate stock information without making unsupported promises.
lessons.why_this_matters: Customers want a reliable answer about whether they can buy an item today. Give the clearest verified answer you have. If the quantity is uncertain, say so and explain the next step.

content_sections.heading: Separate facts from estimates
content_sections.text: A shelf check is a verified observation. An expected delivery date may be an estimate. Do not promise a shipment or hold unless the store’s policy and system support it.

content_sections.heading: Offer a useful next step
content_sections.text: Check approved locations, request a stock check, or connect the customer with a team member who can confirm ordering options. Ask before suggesting a substitute because size or compatibility may matter.

content_sections.heading: Close the loop
content_sections.text: If you promise to check, tell the customer what you found or who will follow up. Do not leave a customer waiting without an update.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer needs eight matching cabinet pulls. Six are confirmed on the shelf. The associate explains that six are available now and asks the inventory lead to check the remaining quantity.
what_to_say_or_do: Offer an approved next step or handoff.
common_mistakes: Promising an arrival date without confirmation.
Substituting a different size without checking fit.
Saying “we have it” based only on a system count.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a supervisor about special orders, reservations, transfers, or uncertain delivery dates.

practice.question: A customer needs eight pulls, but you can verify six. Which response is best?

options.text: Six are here; I can check whether we have two more.
You should buy a different style.

practice.explanation: A clear verified quantity plus a next step builds trust.
